'''''Rumex crispus''''', the '''curly dock''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUCR|taxon=Rumex crispus|access-date=26 October 2015}}</ref> '''curled dock''' or '''yellow dock''', is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Polygonaceae]], native to [[Europe]] and [[Western Asia]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Flora of North America: Magnoliophyta: Caryophyllidae, pt. 2|chapter=Rumex crispus|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-19-522211-1|page=522|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NURmQDm_dJsC&pg=PA522}}</ref>

== Description ==
The plant produces an inflorescence or flower stalk that grows to {{Convert|1.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} high.<ref name="Elias-2009">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=121|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}}</ref> It has smooth leaves shooting off from a large [[basal rosette]], with distinctive waved or curled edges; these can grow to {{Convert|14-24|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}}.<ref name="Elias-2009" /> On the stalk, flowers and seeds are produced in clusters on branched stems, with the largest cluster being found at the apex. The seeds are shiny, brown and encased in the [[sepal|calyx]] of the flower that produced them. This casing enables the seeds to float on water and get caught in wool and animal fur, and this helps the seeds spread to new locations.<ref>Richard H. Uva, Joseph C. Neal and Joseph M. Ditomaso, ''Weeds of The Northeast'', (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1997), Pp. 286-287.</ref> The root structure is a large, yellow, forking [[taproot]].

''Rumex crispus'' has a number of subspecies with distinctive habitat preferences. ''R. crispus'' ssp. ''crispus'' occurs on waste and cultivated ground. ''R. crispus'' ssp. ''littoreus'' has a coastal distribution, and ''R. crispus'' ssp. ''uliginosus'' occurs on tidal estuarine mud.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book | last=Stace | first=C. A. | author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010 |title=New Flora of the British Isles | edition=Third |publisher=Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, U.K. | page=450 | isbn=978-0-521-70772-5 }}</ref> The species hybridizes readily with other ''Rumex'' species including ''[[Rumex obtusifolius]]'', ''[[Rumex obovatus]]'', ''[[Rumex palustris]]'' and ''[[Rumex maritimus]]''.<ref name=Stace />

==Distribution==
Native across temperate Eurasia, and widespread as an introduced species in North America and other temperate regions.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.48059 | title=Rumex crispus (Curled dock) | journal=Cabi Compendium | year=2022 | s2cid=253614635 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Rumexcrispus.jpg|thumb|alt=Fruits of curled dock, showing typical arrowhead shape|Fruits of curled dock (''R. crispus'')]]

Curly dock grows in a wide variety of habitats, including disturbed soil, waste areas, roadsides, fields/meadows, shorelines, and forest edges.<ref>{{cite book |title=Flora of North America: Magnoliophyta: Caryophyllidae, pt. 2|chapter=Rumex crispus|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-19-522211-1|page=523|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NURmQDm_dJsC&pg=PA523}}</ref>
It is widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] throughout the temperate world and has become a serious [[invasive species]] in many areas, including throughout [[North America]], southern [[South America]], [[New Zealand]] and parts of [[Australia]]. It spreads through the seeds contaminating crop seeds, and sticking to clothing. It is classified as an "injurious weed" under the UK [[Weeds Act 1959]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/wild-plants-dangerous-invasive-and-protected-species#dealing-with-injurious-weeds-and-invasive-plants|title=[Withdrawn] Wild plants: dangerous, invasive and protected species – Detailed guidance – GOV.UK|work=www.gov.uk|date=11 December 2014 }}</ref> In the United States, it is classified as a noxious weed in the states of [[Arkansas]] and [[Iowa]].<ref name="Rumex Crispus - USDA">{{cite web |title=Rumex Crispus |url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=RUCR |website=usda.gov |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=11 November 2019}}</ref> It is often seen in disturbed soils at the edges of roadsides, railway beds, and car parks.

=== Host plant ===
The curled dock is an optimal host plant for certain [[Lepidoptera]] species including, ''[[Agrotis ipsilon]]'' (black cutworm). Adult moths [[Oviparity|oviposit]] on these dense, low-lying leaves during the spring/summer season.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Busching |first1=M. K. |last2=Turpin |first2=F. T. |date=1976-10-01 |title=Oviposition Preferences of Black Cutworm Moths Among Various Crop Plants, Weeds, and Plant Debris12 |journal=Journal of Economic Entomology |language=en |volume=69 |issue=5 |pages=587–590 |doi=10.1093/jee/69.5.587 |issn=1938-291X}}</ref>

== Uses and toxicity ==
It can be used as a wild leaf vegetable; the young leaves should be boiled in several changes of water to remove as much of the [[oxalic acid]] in the leaves as possible or can be added directly to salads in moderate amounts.<ref>Lee Allen Peterson, ''Edible Wild Plants'', (New York City: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1977), p. 154.</ref> Once the plant matures it becomes too bitter to consume. Dock leaves are an excellent source of both [[vitamin A]] and [[vitamin C]], as well as a source of [[iron]] and [[potassium]].<ref>http://nutritiondata.self.com/facts/vegetables-and-vegetable-products/2734/2 "Nutritional Facts and Analysis of Dock, raw"</ref> Curly dock leaves are somewhat tart due to the presence of high levels of oxalic acid, and although quite palatable, this plant should only be consumed in moderation as it can irritate the urinary tract and increase the risk of developing [[kidney stone]]s.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} It should be used with care during lactation, as it may cause a laxative effect in the infant.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}}

In Armenia the young plants are harvested and dried and to make a product called Aveluk (ավելուկ). During drying fermentation takes place to make it less bitter. The dried plants are braided into rings and sold. Aveluk is used extensively in Armenian cookery as the basis of salads and soups for which it is reconstituted by boiling in water.<ref>https://www.jidlonacestach.cz/en/aveluk/ "Food on the Move: Aveluk: Wild Sorrel"</ref><ref>https://foragerchef.com/aveluk/ "ForagerChef: Aveluk: Armenian Dried Wild Sorrel (Dock)"</ref>

The seeds of the yellow dock, once dried thoroughly, are edible as well.<ref>Thayer, Samuel, March 1, 2010. ''Nature's Garden: A Guide to Identifying, Harvesting, and Preparing Wild Plants'' Forager's Harvest Press</ref> The dark-brown to black seed [[Glossary of plant morphology#Fruit types|pods]] remain on the stalk until the spring when leaves start growing again. While many wild foraged grains must be [[winnowed]], the pods of ''Rumex crispus'' are small enough that it is more efficient to grind them with the grain. The resulting flour<ref name="Elias-2009" /> is much like [[buckwheat]] in flavor, and while some may find it too bitter, many prefer the seeds over the tartness of the leaves.

In Western herbalism, the root is often used for treating [[anemia]], due to its high level of iron.<ref>Lust, John B.. The herb book. New York: B. Lust Publications, 1974.</ref> It can be powdered and given in capsules, often in combination with stinging nettle (''[[Urtica dioica]]''). This is a classic combination with the plant. Both the leaves and root may be [[laxative]] in some individuals, though not in all, and generally it is mild. This is due to the presence of anthroquinone [[Glycoside|glycosides]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/d/docks-15.html#yel|title=A Modern Herbal - Docks|work=botanical.com}}</ref> and is not an action that should be relied upon, but seen as a possible effect of the plant when taken. The plant may also cause intestinal discomfort to some people. The plant will help with skin conditions if taken internally or applied externally to things like itching, [[scrofula]], and sores.{{citation needed|date=April 2015}} Some studies show that certain [[Anthraquinones|anthroquinones]] can help stop or slow cancer growth, but this may or may not apply to the ones in yellow dock.

Yellow dock is part of the homeopathic [[pharmacopoeia]]. It is used mainly for respiratory conditions, specifically those with a tickling cough that is worse when exposed to cold air. It mentions also passing pains, excessive itching, and that it helps [[Enlarged lymph node|enlarged lymphs]].<ref>[http://abchomeopathy.com/r.php/Rumx "Rumex Crispus." - Homeopathic Remedies. N.p., n.d. Web. 3 Mar. 2014]</ref>

The [[Zuni people]] apply a [[poultice]] of the powdered root to sores, rashes and skin infections, and use [[infusion]] of the root for [[athlete's foot]].<ref>Camazine, Scott and Robert A. Bye 1980 A Study Of The Medical Ethnobotany Of The Zuni Indians of New Mexico. Journal of Ethnopharmacology 2:365-388 (p. 378)</ref>
